lesson.title: Arguments and Types
lesson.summary: Why argument data needs a type, and what happens when it gets the wrong one.

stage.name: Object Core
stage.subtitle: Book chapters 3–4
stage.description: Classes and objects, constructors, visibility, inheritance, abstract classes, interfaces, traits, and exceptions.

payload.markdown: A type determines the way data can be managed in your scripts. You use the string type to display character data, for example, and manipulate such data with string functions. Integers are used in mathematical expressions, Booleans are used in test expressions, and so on. These categories are known as primitive types. On a higher level, though, a class defines a type. A ShopProduct object, therefore, belongs to the primitive type object, but it also belongs to the ShopProduct class type. In this section, I will look at types of both kinds in relation to class methods.

payload.markdown: Method and function definitions do not necessarily require that an argument should be of a particular type. This is both a curse and a blessing. The fact that an argument can be of any type offers you flexibility. You can build methods that respond intelligently to different data types, tailoring functionality to changing circumstances. This flexibility can also cause ambiguity to creep into code when a method body expects an argument to hold one type but gets another.

items: Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Functions: Reusable blocks of code that take arguments and return values.
Primitive Types: int, float, string and bool: PHP's scalar building blocks.
Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
Arrow Functions: fn() => expressions: closures with automatic by-value capture.
Data Mapper: A layer that moves objects to and from storage without the object knowing SQL.
Git, CI & Build: Version control plus automated checks that run on every change.
